posts.title: A Snowflake proxy built from e-waste: one month in the field
posts.description: Early release: this entry is still in production. Its figures run to 16 November, and it will get the updates listed at the end . A Snowflake proxy lets people in censored countries reach Tor through someone else’s internet connection. Mine has run since 20 October, set up as described in part one , on hardware that was on its way out: a Raspberry Pi from 2012 that had been sitting in a drawer, a network cable with a broken plug, an old phone charger. After a month I can say three things about it. It costs nothing I would notice, on my line or on the Pi. Most of its users arrive from Iran and Russia, and their day sets its rhythm. And the version that came with my Linux distribution may be what decides whether it still works for users in Russia.

posts.title: Who actually did it: attribution in Endpoint Security events
posts.description: Part one ended with a justified question. On 3 November, at 23:47 in the evening, my Mac sent a burst of events to my Splunk index, the log search system in my home lab. The events were about privacy permissions, which macOS keeps in a system called TCC (Transparency, Consent and Control). Each event named three processes. Terminal was the app whose permission had changed. sandboxd , the macOS daemon that enforces app sandboxes, was named as the initiator of the change. tccd , the daemon that keeps the TCC records, was the process that reported it.

posts.title: Apple's own endpoint sensor, without an agent
posts.description: I went looking for the best way to monitor the security of my personal macOS environment, and it turned into an in-depth investigation of how much eslogger can tell about a Mac. The environment has three Macs in it, and I started with one. The one this series begins with is a MacBook Air (15-inch, M3, 2024), which goes everywhere with me. It carries my work: the code I am working on, my research, the security events I review, architecture work and some limited penetration testing, along with confidential findings that could do harm in the wrong hands. It carries the rest of my life too, and some of other people’s. On it I talk to prospects and customers, message everyone I know, the people closest to me included, keep a journal, read about things that touch on how I am doing, and edit documents I would not want anyone else to open.
